title: Ewedu
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Jute leaf boiled two minutes, then eight to ten more with locust bean, and pulsed — not blended — with only half a cup of the cooking water, so it stays semi-pureed rather than smooth.
longDesc: Ewedu is the slippery green half of abula. The traditional tool is the ijabe, a small broom that pounds the leaves in the pot until they break into tiny pieces — and the point of it is draw, not smoothness. That is why a whisk substitutes perfectly well and a blender overdelivers. This version uses the pulse function deliberately, to a semi-puree, and it uses no potash at all: the author says so outright and relies on the blending for viscosity instead.
ingredients: 1 bouillon cube (half a crayfish-flavoured cube used in the original)
steps: Pick the leaves off without the stalk or stem. Only the leaf goes in.
Bring the 2 cups of water to a rolling boil on medium heat.
Add the leaves and boil 2 minutes.
Add the locust beans and continue boiling until tender, roughly 8 to 10 minutes.
Take it off the heat and let it cool briefly.
Transfer to the blender with the iru and only 1/2 cup of the cooking water — not all of it.
Pulse to a semi-pureed consistency. Do not blend smooth.
Return to the pan with the crayfish, bouillon and salt.
Off the heat, let it simmer 3 minutes on the residual heat, stirring.
chefTips: Only half a cup of the boiling water goes into the blender. Tip all of it in and you get soup instead of ewedu.
Pulse, do not blend. The ijabe breaks the leaves into pieces; it does not puree them. A whisk does the same job — the author says it 'functions just as good as an Ijabe'.
No potash here, and that is a deliberate position: 'I don't cook with Kaun (Potash), but rest assured, blending does enhance the viscosity.' For the version that does use it, see NGA118.
Stems make it stringy. Strip them.
The last 3 minutes are on residual heat with the stove off. Boiling it after the crayfish goes in dulls the green.
Ewedu is served beside gbegiri rather than mixed into it — the mixing happens on the plate.
If it will not draw, you under-boiled the leaves. Tender is the condition, not the clock.
commonMistakes: Pouring all the cooking water into the blend.
Boiling it hard after the crayfish is in.
Adding potash by default when the recipe is built not to need it.
sources: Adapted from 'Ewedu Soup Recipe', byline Sisi Jemimah — the 1 big bunch to 2 cups water, the 2-minute first boil, the 8-to-10-minute boil with iru, the half cup of water into the blender, the pulse-to-semi-pureed instruction and the 3-minute residual-heat finish are all as printed there.

The refusal of potash is hers and is quoted on the page: 'Now, I don't cook with Kaun (Potash), but rest assured. blending does enhance the viscosity.' She also offers a whisk as an ijabe substitute — 'it functions just as good as an Ijabe'.

The ijabe mechanism is from 9jafoodie's 'Ewedu Elegusi' page (byline absent): 'this step is traditionally done with a local broom called "Ijabe". The broom is used to pound the cooking ewedu until leaves are broken into tiny pieces.'

DISAGREEMENT on potash, not reconciled. Sisi Jemimah refuses it outright. 9jafoodie's ewedu does not mention it and thickens with a tablespoon of blended egusi instead (NGA003). Tribune Online's Testimony Ishola calls for a 'tiny amount of potash or baking soda'; a second Tribune article specifies a teaspoon (NGA118). Notably, 9jafoodie uses no kaun in ewedu but half a teaspoon in okra (NGA015) — a split within one site.

DISAGREEMENT on the ratio: 9jafoodie gives 6 packed cups of leaves to 1 cup of water; this recipe gives 1 big bunch to 2 cups with only half a cup carried into the blend. Boil times also differ, 5 minutes against 8 to 10.

The alkali's function is confirmed but not explained by any source consulted. 'Understanding Nigerian Condiments - Kaun (Akanwa)' on Funke Koleosho's blog (post byline 'tasteofnigeria') lists ewedu under 'vegetable enhancement' without saying why it works. See NGA120.
reheating: Gentle heat with a splash of water. Do not boil.
healthBenefits: Jute leaf is high in vitamins A, C and E and in calcium.
Very low in calories and fat.
The mucilage is a soluble fibre.
culturalNote: Ewedu is Corchorus — the same jute leaf eaten as molokhia across Egypt and the Levant, and it travels under that name in Middle Eastern shops. Across Nigerian languages it is ewedu in Yoruba, kerenkere in Igbo and rama or ayoyo in Hausa. In Yorubaland it is almost never eaten alone: it goes on the plate with gbegiri and a stew, and the three together are abula.
